title: Who cares for our streets? Maintenance, responsibility and everyday pride
label: 3 November 2026 · Maintenance and enforcement in public spaces
summary: Witnesses from Central, Create Streets and Clean Up Britain gave practical, experience‑based evidence about why everyday public spaces look and feel worse, who currently (doesn't) take responsibility, how culture and design interact, and what immediate, medium and long-term steps could help: clearer local accountability, simpler rules, more visible local roles, and renewed investment in maintenance and civic education.

chapters.title: What do we mean by public space — and what's the committee's exam question?
chapters.takeaway: Public space means where people live, move and meet; the committee should ask who is accountable and what would make maintenance reliable and visible.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Two framing questions: first, how do you define the public realm or public space? Second, what's the single 'exam question' this inquiry should answer?

turns.speaker: David Milner
turns.text: We design streets, manuals and codes across the UK. 'Public realm' for me is the streets and spaces where people move and meet — pavements, shopfronts, trees, bins and signage.

turns.speaker: Patricia Brown
turns.text: I see public realm as where we congregate and live our daily lives: roads, pavements, parks, play areas and the civic spaces that shape whether people choose to live and spend there.

turns.speaker: Ed Lennox
turns.text: Clean Up Britain focuses on litter and fly-tipping but that sits within the wider public realm: the maintenance, the visible care and the accountability for those places.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: So the committee's exam question should focus on ownership and accountability for maintenance, and what practical steps create dependable, well-cared-for spaces?

chapters.title: How bad is it — perception, evidence and causes
chapters.takeaway: People overwhelmingly feel public spaces are worse; causes are mixed design, weakened local leadership, complex responsibilities, underfunding and cultural change.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Are public spaces definitely worse, and how do we know?

turns.speaker: David Milner
turns.text: I can't point to a single national deterioration dataset, but polling and repeated local feedback show pavement quality, bins and visual clutter are top concerns.

turns.speaker: Ed Lennox
turns.text: Surveys show public perception is strongly negative. We also see practical failures: bridges with tree roots, unrepaired roadworks and a huge number of fly-tips with few prosecutions.

turns.speaker: Patricia Brown
turns.text: Many gains were made since the 1990s, but austerity, fragmented waste systems and the 'takeaway/leave-behind' culture eroded maintenance and public care.

turns.speaker: Lord Cameron of Dillington
turns.text: Does quality vary around the country and between rural and urban areas?

turns.speaker: Ed Lennox
turns.text: Yes — rural areas often have more fragmented ownership (parish, county, National Highways) so responsibility is disputed; it's simpler in urban areas but still inconsistent.

turns.speaker: Patricia Brown
turns.text: There are great and poor examples everywhere; the difference is often accidental — the presence of strong local civic leadership or the reverse.

turns.speaker: David Milner
turns.text: Regional differences also reflect funding and governance patterns: who holds the highways budget, whether there's devolved funding, and local entrepreneurial leaders.

chapters.title: Who is responsible — systems, culture and everyday competence
chapters.takeaway: Responsibility is spread across too many bodies; people see visible failures as signs the state doesn't care. Rebuilding local agency and clearer duties matters.

turns.speaker: Lord Bailey of Paddington
turns.text: Do degraded spaces feed wider political narratives about neglect and care?

turns.speaker: Patricia Brown
turns.text: Yes. Poorly maintained places tell residents they are not valued. That shapes political narratives and trust in local representatives.

turns.speaker: David Milner
turns.text: First impressions matter — stations, streets and airports signal competence. Everyday 'street scars' — patched pavements, phone boxes, bins — show a lack of ownership.

turns.speaker: Ed Lennox
turns.text: The law makes dropping litter and fly-tipping criminal, but detection and penalties are minimal. People rarely get caught; fines are low and enforcement scarce.

turns.speaker: Baroness Miller of Chilthorne Domer
turns.text: Dog fouling has improved. What lessons help change behaviour?

turns.speaker: Ed Lennox
turns.text: Behaviour change came from unceasing public messages and enforcement; we've lost consistent civic messaging. Education, starting in schools, matters hugely.

turns.speaker: David Milner
turns.text: Design shapes culture: if streets are built for cars rather than walking, people won't take care. Amsterdam changed design first, then culture shifted.

turns.speaker: Patricia Brown
turns.text: Agency matters: where people feel ownership they treat places better. Business improvement districts, heritage projects and local champions show how civic pride is revived.

turns.speaker: Lord Porter of Spalding
turns.text: Councils have tight budgets — 87% on social care etc. Is lack of money the main problem?

turns.speaker: Ed Lennox
turns.text: It's not just lack of money; it's poor spending and fragmented contracts. There's enough public money overall but not the local accountability and competence to spend it well.

chapters.title: Practical solutions: clearer accountability, local roles and quick wins
chapters.takeaway: Practical steps include one clear local owner for public realm stretches, reviving local 'lengthspeople', simpler rules for community action, smarter enforcement and shining a light on good practice.

turns.speaker: Baroness Barran
turns.text: If you could start a five-year plan, what are two or three catalytic actions?

turns.speaker: Patricia Brown
turns.text: Create simplified local ownership — a single responsible body with budget and staff — and spotlight where it works so other places can copy it. Keep people 'on the streets' rather than outsourcing everything to cameras.

turns.speaker: Ed Lennox
turns.text: Three practical steps: 1) a ministerial champion for the public realm to coordinate nationally; 2) revive local lengthspeople who own stretches of place; 3) insist independent sign-off that roadworks and site clearances are properly completed before contractors are paid.

turns.speaker: David Milner
turns.text: Lower regulatory barriers to local action — e.g., a 'right to plant' outside your home — and fix perverse incentives such as anachronistic low fines in the New Roads and Street Works Act 1991 that encourage slow, poor-quality reinstatement.

turns.speaker: Lord Ravensdale
turns.text: How do we move from perception to evidence so we can measure improvement?

turns.speaker: Ed Lennox
turns.text: There are national surveys (Keep Britain Tidy and others) and local reporting. We should collect consistent metrics on litter, fly-tips, roadwork reinstatement and maintenance backlogs and publish them.

turns.speaker: Baroness Griffin of Princethorpe
turns.text: Any underexplored areas the committee should probe?

turns.speaker: Patricia Brown
turns.text: Look at equity: map who lacks access to good public space and how management failures affect mobility-impaired or low-income communities; study long-term stewardship models, not one-off redesigns.

turns.speaker: Ed Lennox
turns.text: Ask the bigger exam question: how do we rebuild trust that public agencies will maintain the public realm? Simplify the number of agencies, and make them enablers for people who want to help.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We asked witnesses to send follow-up evidence. David had to leave for another committee but will return written notes; Patricia and Ed will provide more concrete case studies and costed ideas such as lengthspeople.

turns.speaker: Patricia Brown
turns.text: One final practical note: small, well-maintained lighting and carefully designed spaces can change how people feel about a place — even one resident saying 'it makes me feel rich' shows the power of small investments in care.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you. The inquiry will press on the central themes: clearer local accountability, simpler rules for civic action, consistent maintenance funding, and rebuilding civic pride through education and design.
